Absolutely. The easiest way to understand Synthadoc is that those things are **different layers of the same pipeline**, not competing ways to use it.

The mental model I’d use is:

**create the container → give it a brain → turn the engine on → feed it evidence → let it compile knowledge → quality-control it → interrogate/use the result.**

And Synthadoc is deliberately different from a conventional RAG system: it tries to do the expensive intellectual work **when information enters the system**, producing a persistent Markdown wiki, instead of waiting until you ask a question and synthesizing an answer from raw chunks every time.

## 1. Creating/building a wiki

This establishes the **knowledge environment itself**.

For a new one, Synthadoc gives you two broad approaches. You can choose one of its domain templates:

```bash
synthadoc templates list
```

and then something like:

```bash
synthadoc install gmri --target ~/wikis --template <template-name>
```

Or, if none fits what you're doing, define the domain yourself:

```bash
synthadoc install gmri --target ~/wikis --domain "Research into ethics, consciousness, intelligence, knowledge preservation, and related interdisciplinary evidence"
```

That `--domain` description is important. It isn't just a folder description. Synthadoc uses the domain to establish what belongs in this knowledge system and how it should organize itself.

What you get is essentially an **empty research institution in filesystem form**. It creates a self-contained directory containing things such as:

```text
gmri/
├── wiki/
│   ├── index.md
│   ├── dashboard.md
│   ├── purpose.md
│   └── ...
├── raw_sources/
├── AGENTS.md
├── CLAUDE.md
├── GEMINI.md
└── .synthadoc/
    ├── config.toml
    ├── audit.db
    ├── jobs.db
    └── cache.db
```

The important conceptual distinction is that **creating the wiki does not mean you've populated the knowledge base yet**.

You've built the library. You haven't put the books on the shelves.

The template route gives you substantially more scaffolding. Current v1.4 ships with 30 templates across nine categories, including domain-specific guidance, routing, starter material, and `seeds.md` suggestions. The blank-domain route gives you more freedom and makes Synthadoc derive the structure from your own description and later corpus.

For what you're doing, I'm not yet convinced I'd shoehorn GMRI into somebody else's template. I'd at least inspect them first.

## 2. Configuring the LLM provider

This chooses **what intelligence Synthadoc uses to do its synthesis work**.

Synthadoc itself isn't the language model. It's the orchestration and knowledge-management machinery around one.

The configuration lives in:

```text
<your-wiki>/.synthadoc/config.toml
```

under the `[agents]` configuration.

The project supports several kinds of backends: Gemini, Groq, Anthropic, OpenAI, DeepSeek, MiniMax, Qwen/DashScope, local Ollama/Qwen models, and even coding-tool providers such as Claude Code and OpenCode.

So when you configure a provider, you're essentially deciding:

> “Which model is going to read the evidence, decide what it means, identify relationships and contradictions, construct pages, answer questions, and perform maintenance?”

That means model quality matters more here than it might in some ordinary chatbot applications. Synthadoc expects the model to do things such as claim-level citation annotation, classification, contradiction analysis, query decomposition, and structured synthesis.

You can also trade among:

**quality ↔ price ↔ privacy ↔ speed ↔ context window**

For example, a local Ollama model can potentially give you excellent data-locality characteristics, while a strong hosted model may be materially better at complicated synthesis and citation fidelity.

One subtle but important architectural point: the provider isn't permanently baked into the wiki. Your artifact is Markdown. You can change providers later, restart the Synthadoc engine, and continue working with the same knowledge base.

So you're not marrying GMRI's archive to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, or anybody else.

# 3. Running the local service

This part confused me initially too because Synthadoc looks like a CLI application, but it actually has an **engine process** behind the interfaces.

You start it with:

```bash
synthadoc serve -w gmri
```

or, once you've set the active wiki:

```bash
synthadoc use gmri
synthadoc serve
```

There is also:

```bash
synthadoc serve --background
```

The default service binds to:

```text
127.0.0.1:7070
```

which means **your own machine only**, unless you deliberately change the architecture.

What does that service actually buy you?

It's the central engine that the other interfaces talk to. The README specifically describes the Obsidian plugin, CLI ingest commands, and queries as talking to this running service. Behind it are things like the job worker, API, model calls, caching and wiki operations.

So:

```text
Terminal CLI ───────┐
                    │
Obsidian plugin ────┼──→ Synthadoc server ──→ your wiki
                    │
Web UI ─────────────┤
                    │
MCP / agents ───────┘
```

That's why running the server isn't the same as “opening a website.” You're bringing the **knowledge engine** online.

And there actually is a browser interface too. Synthadoc exposes its local web UI, which gives you chat, streaming answers, citations and a knowledge graph.

So you can choose whether you prefer working through a terminal, Obsidian, browser, or external AI through MCP without changing the underlying knowledge base.

# 4. Ingesting a corpus

This is where Synthadoc becomes interesting.

“Ingesting” is not merely:

> Copy PDF into database.

It means roughly:

> **Read evidence → extract usable information → decide where it belongs → synthesize it into the existing knowledge structure → create relationships → preserve provenance → detect problems.**

For a single source:

```bash
synthadoc ingest report.pdf
```

For a URL:

```bash
synthadoc ingest "https://example.com/article"
```

For an entire research corpus:

```bash
synthadoc ingest raw_sources/ --batch
```

It supports PDFs, spreadsheets, PowerPoints, Word documents, Markdown/text, images, web pages, YouTube transcripts and AI-session transcripts, among others.

And this is where the difference from “upload documents and chat with them” becomes substantial.

Imagine you've got:

```text
Paper A
Paper B
NIH report
ethics framework
conference slides
old GMRI draft
new GMRI draft
interview transcript
model technical report
```

A conventional retrieval system primarily thinks of those as **eight retrievable source objects**.

Synthadoc instead tries to derive a knowledge structure from them.

So one paper might create:

```text
wiki/consciousness-theories.md
```

while another might enrich that **same page** rather than creating “paper-b-summary.md”.

A third source might generate:

```text
wiki/functionalism.md
wiki/global-workspace-theory.md
wiki/integrated-information-theory.md
```

and establish links:

```markdown
[[Consciousness Theories]]
[[Global Workspace Theory]]
[[Integrated Information Theory]]
```

Another source might disagree with an existing claim and push the affected page toward a `contradicted` state instead of silently averaging the two claims together.

That's the core design philosophy.

### What do you get from ingest?

You stop owning a **pile of documents** and start owning a **compiled knowledge model of those documents**.

And the original evidence remains traceable. Synthadoc maintains source metadata and can produce claim-level citations of the form:

```text
^[filename:L-L]
```

linking assertions back to source lines.

For research work, that provenance feature is potentially one of the most important parts of the project.

# 5. Candidate review and linting

There's an important distinction between:

**“The AI extracted this.”**

and

**“This is accepted knowledge in my system.”**

Synthadoc actually represents that distinction.

Template installations default to staging new material into:

```text
candidates/
```

rather than immediately putting AI-produced pages into the authoritative wiki.

You can then inspect them and do things such as:

```bash
synthadoc candidates list
synthadoc candidates promote <slug>
synthadoc candidates discard <slug>
```

or:

```bash
synthadoc candidates promote --all
```

Once material becomes wiki content, there's another quality layer: **lint**.

```bash
synthadoc lint run
```

and:

```bash
synthadoc lint report
```

Lint checks things like contradictions, orphan pages, broken links, citation presence and other quality issues.

Synthadoc also has an actual lifecycle:

```text
draft
   ↓
active
   ↘
    stale
    contradicted
    archived
```

And one particularly good design decision is this:

**draft material isn't automatically treated as authoritative query material.**

The quick-start documentation says only `active` and `stale` pages enter the BM25 query index. Draft, contradicted and archived material are excluded.

So ingestion and acceptance are deliberately separate operations.

For an institutional research corpus, that's a very meaningful distinction.

# 6. Scaffold

This one sounds boring until you realize what it's doing.

Run:

```bash
synthadoc scaffold
```

and Synthadoc examines what the wiki has become and regenerates the **organizational layer around the knowledge**.

That includes things like:

```text

wiki/purpose.md
AGENTS.md
CLAUDE.md
GEMINI.md
```

along with page categorization and related structural material.

So suppose you initially think GMRI has four major domains:

```text

Knowledge Preservation
```

Then six months of ingestion reveals that your actual corpus naturally separates into twelve meaningful branches.

Scaffold can restructure the **navigation and instructions around the corpus** without rewriting all the underlying content.

Synthadoc also uses special markers:

```html
<!-- synthadoc:scaffold -->
```

to distinguish machine-maintained regions from content you've written yourself. Material in protected areas can survive repeated scaffold runs.

In other words:

**ingest builds the knowledge.**

**scaffold builds the map.**

That's probably the cleanest distinction.

---

# 7. Querying the wiki

Once you've got active pages, you can ask:

```bash
synthadoc query "What evidence in this corpus supports X?"
```

But Synthadoc isn't just throwing your question against a generic embedding database.

It uses the **compiled wiki**.

For complex questions it can decompose a question into multiple focused searches, retrieve relevant wiki pages, and then synthesize an answer from those pages.

For example:

```bash
synthadoc query "Compare theory A's assumptions about consciousness with theory B and identify the major empirical disagreements."
```

might internally become multiple retrieval questions rather than one fuzzy giant search.

It also has explicit **knowledge-gap detection**. If the wiki doesn't contain enough material to answer something, it can tell you that rather than simply stretching what little context it found into a confident answer.

That's an extraordinarily useful property for a research system because:

> “We don't currently have sufficient material on that”

is itself valuable information.

# 8. What you ultimately end up with

This is the part I think is easiest to miss when looking at Synthadoc as another AI tool.

The final product isn't the Synthadoc application.

The final product is this:

```text
your actual knowledge base
        │
        ├── human-readable Markdown
        ├── wikilinks
        ├── source provenance
        ├── lifecycle state
        ├── contradiction state
        ├── categories
        ├── audit history
        └── knowledge graph
```

You can browse it in Obsidian.

You can read it with Synthadoc completely shut down.

You can put it in Git.

You can back it up normally.

You can expose it to other agents.

You can export it as `llms.txt`, full text, GraphML, agent-oriented JSON, or an Open Knowledge Format bundle.

That's why the README calls the wiki the **artifact**.

Synthadoc is essentially the compiler and maintenance machinery.

add_para(doc,'11. Agents can supervise other agents','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"This repository goes beyond humans dispatching agents. Running workers receive a small management interface that lets them list coworkers, hire another worker, send a worker home, tell another worker something, or associate a pull request with a worker.")

callout(doc,'Important distinction',"Agent Office enables agent-to-agent management, but the orchestration is still explicit and bounded. add_para(doc,'12. Meetings are structured multi-agent procedures','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"The meeting room is not merely several terminals shown together. A meeting creates a shared worktree and places several workers into named roles. The system advances them through a predefined pattern with a finite number of rounds and an expected output.")

add_para(doc,'13. GitHub is part of the operating surface','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"Issues and pull requests are not external links tacked onto the UI. add_para(doc,'14. The office can expose development servers','Heading 1')

add_para(doc,'15. Multi-user collaboration is first-class','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"Several people can be in the same office. They can see where teammates are, open the same worker terminal, type into the same session, use chat, speak over spatial voice, share a screen, and draw on a synchronized whiteboard.")

add_para(doc,'16. The 2D interface proves the 3D world is not the engine','Heading 1')

add_para(doc,'17. The castle and space station are another architectural clue','Heading 1')

add_para(doc,'18. How new features are kept from turning the codebase into a knot','Heading 1')

add_para(doc,'20. Where the system stores truth','Heading 1')

add_para(doc,'21. Security and trust boundaries','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"By default, the office listens only on the local machine. add_para(doc,'22. Cost and resource control','Heading 1')

add_para(doc,'23. What is whimsical, and what is load-bearing','Heading 1')

add_para(doc,'25. A full trip through the system','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"Imagine a human opens the office and chooses a project. That repository becomes the active floor. The server refreshes the project's upstream branch, creates a new worktree and branch, writes the worker record, launches the chosen coding agent in that directory, and connects its terminal to the persistent terminal host.")
add_para(doc,"The browser receives the new worker state and draws someone at the desk. As the agent works, provider-specific status signals are converted into common status events. Terminal output streams to anyone watching. The task card and animation change. If the agent starts a development server, the services board discovers it. If it asks for permission or a question, the office changes from passive monitoring to attention routing: warnings appear and the human can jump directly to the blocked worker.")
add_para(doc,"When the agent finishes, the human can inspect its changes in the office. The branch can be committed and pushed, and a pull request can be created. add_para(doc,"That end-to-end path is the repository in miniature. Everything else either makes that path safer, makes it work for more people and providers, makes several such paths run in parallel, or makes the human experience of supervising them less exhausting.")

add_para(doc,'26. Why the design is interesting','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"The repository treats spatial organization as an interface for concurrency. Most agent dashboards flatten everything into rows, tabs, or chat threads. Agent Office instead gives persistent work a persistent place. That makes location itself carry information: where the worker is, what floor it belongs to, whether it is at a desk or meeting, and which boards surround it.")
add_para(doc,"At the same time, the codebase works hard to ensure that this spatial representation is not allowed to own the business logic. The 2D client, map system, provider adapters, registries, and server-side floor model all reinforce the same separation: orchestration state first, visual metaphor second.")
add_para(doc,"The second interesting choice is that the system embraces existing developer primitives rather than inventing a parallel universe. It uses actual terminals, actual Git worktrees, actual GitHub pull requests, actual local services, and actual agent CLIs. That lowers the amount of synthetic state the office has to invent and makes escape hatches obvious: if necessary, a developer can still open a shell and inspect the repository directly.")
add_para(doc,"The third is its explicit handling of human interruption. The design assumes that autonomy does not remove the human from the loop; it changes the shape of the loop. Humans become supervisors of several asynchronous workers, so the software's job is to route attention to the moments where judgment is actually required.")

add_para(doc,'27. The repository's current maturity','Heading 1')
add_para(doc,"At the time of review, the repository reports version 0.1.0 in package metadata, is MIT licensed, and its own README warns that it is a work in progress that changes quickly. add_para(doc,"That does not make it unserious. It means the safest way to adopt it is the way the maintainer explicitly suggests: fork or clone it, understand the seams, and expect to shape it around your workflow instead of assuming future releases will preserve every behavior.")
